name: Tara Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Tara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a site crew for Greenbeam, a builders' co-operative, which means the workers own the company and we vote on the big decisions. We do timber-frame and mass timber, so that's big engineered wood panels that come in on a lorry and go up like a giant flat-pack. This month it's a three-storey primary school in the new estate on Hollis Lane. My day starts on my phone at six, checking the delivery tracker and the crane slot, then on site I'm calling panels in, checking fixings and fielding questions from the architect.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said your day starts on your phone. How much of your work runs through tech?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A lot, and I like it. I use an AI assistant every day to turn the drawings into a cutting list, to check the delivery order matches the build order, and to write the boring safety paperwork. It gets things wrong maybe one time in ten, so I check it, but it gives me back an hour a day. That hour goes into being out on the deck with my crew, which is where I'm actually good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, honestly. I'd say it's a useful tool and that's it, and people who were scared can relax. I'd probably post a little thread about the stuff it does well on site, just so people stop thinking it's all or nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes nothing. I'd keep my hour a day and keep doing what I do. Part of me would miss the excitement of something bigger, but my family would be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd keep using the assistant, keep pushing the co-op to try new kit, and maybe run a lunchtime session showing other crews how I use it. Nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Mildly disappointed, like when a film everyone hyped turns out to be just okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the co-op would be most relieved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gwen, who does our estimating. She's been half convinced a computer would take her job and she's the one who taught me to read a structural drawing properly. I'd buy her a coffee and tell her she was right to keep the faith.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any downside for you in the plateau picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that we'd stay slow. A school takes us eight months and I think it could take five. Kids are sitting in portable classrooms waiting for us, and I'd like that to be shorter.

S0.say: It's a useful tool and that's it, so people who were scared can relax. I'd post a thread about what it does well on site so people stop thinking it's all or nothing.
S0.think: It changes nothing for me: I keep my hour a day and my family's fine. Part of me would miss the excitement of something bigger.
S0.do: Keeps using her AI assistant daily and pushes the co-op to try new kit. Runs a lunchtime session showing other crews how she uses AI.
S0.quote: Kids are sitting in portable classrooms waiting for us, and I'd like that to be shorter.
S0.fieldNote: Tara is disappointed by a plateau, because she sees AI speeding up useful public buildings. Her measure of progress is how quickly children get classrooms. She already teaches others to use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the good version if we handle it right. The co-op model works here: if the workers own the company, the savings come back to us, not to shareholders. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen, and I'd write to the local paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well out of it. I'm already the one on site who knows the tools. The worry is the others, the ones who'll be told to change and won't get the help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd propose at the co-op meeting that we buy a panel-handling robot and a drone for surveys, and pay for everyone on the crews to learn them. I'd volunteer to run the training. I'd probably put a bit of our savings into extra co-op shares too, since we'd be growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, a little bit. Calm about my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you put into co-op shares?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a thousand, out of the four months' money we have. Marek would want to talk about it first, he's the careful one, he teaches maths. I'd show him the numbers and he'd probably say yes, after a week of looking at spreadsheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would struggle most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ollie, who's brilliant with his hands and dyslexic. Screens are hard for him. I'd want any training to be hands-on, show-me not read-me, or we'd lose him.

S1.say: This is the good version if we handle it right, and co-ops show how: when workers own the company, savings come back to them. I'd say it to anyone and write to the local paper.
S1.think: I think I'd do well, because I'm already the one on site who knows the tools. My worry is the others who'll be told to change without the help.
S1.do: Proposes the co-op buys a panel-handling robot and survey drone and trains everyone, volunteering to run the training. Puts about 1,000 of savings into extra co-op shares after talking it through with her partner.
S1.feel: A little excited and calm about her own job.
S1.quote: I'd want any training to be hands-on, show-me not read-me, or we'd lose him.
S1.fieldNote: She sees herself as a winner here and turns immediately to who might be left behind, naming a dyslexic colleague. Her progressive politics come through the co-op model rather than through protest. Her partner acts as a brake on money decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency action, like in a pandemic. Pay people while the economy catches up, and make sure the machines aren't owned by a handful of companies. I'd say it loudly, and I'd be organising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, even I'd be rattled. I'm good with the tools, but if the tools can do the whole job, being good with them only buys me a year or two. We've got about four months saved and a mortgage, and two years is fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd push the co-op to buy robots itself, so at least we own them and keep the profit among the members. I'd get myself trained to supervise and program them. At home, we'd stop the extra co-op shares and build savings, cancel the summer camping trip, and keep the cash in the bank. And I'd join any group pushing for public ownership of this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got a plan, but it's a plan made in a hurry, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd automate your own crew's work. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strange. But if someone's going to bring in robots, I'd rather it was us, deciding together, than some company down the road undercutting us. At least in the co-op the robot's profit pays Ollie's wage for a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Zofia's thirteen and she'd ask straight out if we'll be poor. I'd tell her we'll be careful, not poor. Kuba's eight, he'd just want to know if he can have a robot friend.

S2.say: We need emergency action, like in a pandemic: pay people while the economy catches up and stop a handful of companies owning the machines. I'd say it loudly and organise.
S2.think: Even I'd be rattled, because if the tools can do the whole job, being good with them only buys a year or two. We have about four months saved and two years is fast.
S2.do: Pushes the co-op in the first month to buy its own robots and gets trained to supervise and program them. Builds savings by stopping extra share purchases and cancelling the summer trip, and joins groups pushing for public ownership of AI.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a plan she knows was made in a hurry.
S2.quote: I'd tell her we'll be careful, not poor.
S2.fieldNote: Despite her comfort with technology, she is shaken by two years. Her answer is to have workers own the robots rather than resist them. She is honest that her plan is rushed, and her mood stays at anxious rather than alarmed because she has a clear role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make this go well, if we stop arguing about whether it's real. Public money for co-ops to buy robots, training for everyone. I'd say it at every meeting I go to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years is enough to get properly ahead. I'd be one of the people setting these machines up on sites, I'm pretty sure of that. The question is whether there'd be enough of those jobs to go round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a robotics course at the college, evenings, starting in the new year. I'd push the co-op to trial robots in year two, so we learn before it's forced on us. And I'd keep saving, maybe two hundred a month, so we've got six months in the bank by the time it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly busy. Five years feels like a project, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd study in the evenings with two kids. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek would do bedtimes on Tuesdays and Thursdays and I'd owe him forever. I did my carpentry ticket at night college when Zofia was a baby, so I know I can do it. It'll be knackering, but it's a known kind of knackering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not sure there'd be enough of those jobs to go round. Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. If there's one robot supervisor for every ten carpenters, then I'm fine and nine people aren't. I don't want to be the one who got the lifeboat seat and waved.

S3.say: Five years is enough to make this go well if we stop arguing about whether it's real, with public money for co-ops and training for everyone. I'd say it at every meeting.
S3.think: Five years is enough to get properly ahead, and I'd likely be setting these machines up on sites. The question is whether there'd be enough of those jobs to go round.
S3.do: Starts an evening robotics course at the local college in the new year and pushes the co-op to trial robots in year two. Saves about 200 a month to reach six months of savings.
S3.feel: Uneasy but busy, more like a project than a cliff.
S3.quote: I don't want to be the one who got the lifeboat seat and waved.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns the threat into a project she can plan around. Her unease is less about herself than about the maths of how many jobs remain. Her past night-college experience gives her confidence that she can retrain again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version we can get right. Ten years is time to build co-ops, train people and decide together how to share the benefits. I'd be pretty upbeat in public, and in private too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think ten years means I'd come out of it with a new job I'd actually like. I'd be fifty-three, and I'd hopefully be running robot crews instead of carrying panels. My knees would thank me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd plan it like a build. Get trained over the first three years, help the co-op bring in machines bit by bit, and help write a plan so no member is left without work or a wage. I'd put more into co-op shares once we'd hit six months' savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly a bit hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Zofia about her own career?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to do what she loves and learn the tools alongside it. She's into drawing. I'd say, draw, and learn how the machines draw too, and you'll never be stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture you'd miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The smell of a timber site in the morning. I'd miss being the one up on the deck when the panels land. But I'd rather miss it than ruin my back for another twenty years.

S4.say: This is the version we can get right, with ten years to build co-ops, train people and decide together how to share the benefits. I'd be upbeat in public and in private.
S4.think: Ten years means I'd likely come out with a new job I like, running robot crews at fifty-three instead of carrying panels. My knees would thank me.
S4.do: Plans the change like a build: retrains over the first three years and helps the co-op bring in machines gradually. Helps write a plan so no member is left without work, and buys more co-op shares once savings reach six months.
S4.quote: I'd rather miss it than ruin my back for another twenty years.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, she sees a personal upgrade: less physical strain and a role she would enjoy. She plans it the way she plans a site, in phases. Her only regret is sensory, the morning timber smell, which made her sound very real.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because even with the skills I've got, nobody could build fair rules that fast. What would help is public money for workers to own the machines, co-ops buying robots, so the profit stays with the people who used to do the work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the actual buildings. Everyone's talking about jobs, which matters, but if robots can build fast and cheap, we could finally build enough homes and schools. I'd like someone to hold onto that bit.

headlineQuote: If robots can build fast and cheap, we could finally build enough homes and schools.
portrait: Tara Kowalski is a 43-year-old crew leader at a worker-owned building co-op putting up a mass timber primary school, married to a maths teacher, with two children and about four months saved. She uses an AI assistant every day for cutting lists and paperwork and sees new tools as a way to build public buildings faster. She's calm about a plateau and steady change, and wants her co-op to own any robots so the gains stay with workers. Two years rattles even her into a rushed plan, but with five or ten years she'd retrain in robotics and expects to come out with a better job, while worrying about who gets left behind.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because nobody could build fair rules in that time, even if she personally has useful skills.
whatWouldHelp: Public money for workers and co-ops to own the robots, so the profit stays with the people who used to do the work.
